_doc:
Domain knowledge about model internals, for DESIGN decisions rather than failure recovery. The rest of the corpus records what broke and how it was fixed; that is necessary and it cannot answer 'what does this request actually require?'. When a prompt says 'build me a transformer' or 'add position encoding', the system needs the shapes, the invariants, and the things a user means but does not say. An entry belongs here when knowing it changes what gets built, not merely how a build is repaired.

EVERY ENTRY CARRIES ITS SOURCE. This is reference knowledge, so it is only as good as where it came from and whether it was checked. `verified_by` states what was actually done to confirm it -- an entry nobody checked is a claim, not corpus.
why_these_matter: A build request is usually under-specified. 'A transformer' silently requires a residual stream of constant width, a scaled dot-product, and a position signal; omit any one and it compiles, trains, and is wrong. These entries name the requirements a prompt leaves implicit so they can be checked rather than assumed.
verification_policy: Mathematical claims are checked by derivation and, where practical, by executing the reference implementation against worked cases. `verified_by` records which. Nothing is admitted on the strength of having been read somewhere.

entries.lesson: Every sublayer of a transformer block reads and writes the SAME tensor shape [seq_len, d_model]. Attention projects out to d_model and the MLP projects up to d_ff then back down to d_model, specifically so the residual stream width never changes. The stack is N identical blocks composed on an unchanging carrier.
entries.why_it_generalizes: It converts an architecture question into a checkable invariant: any block that does not return [seq_len, d_model] is wrong regardless of what it computes internally. That is testable without a corpus of examples and without training anything, so it is a cheap oracle for generated model code.

shapes.Q, K, V: [seq_len, d_model], split per head to [seq_len, d_head]

implied_requirements: scores scaled by 1/sqrt(d_head), not 1/sqrt(d_model) -- the scale follows the head, not the model
d_model must divide evenly by n_heads or the per-head split is silently ragged
output projection W_O exists to bring concatenated heads back to d_model; omitting it appears to work at n_heads=1
entries.used_when: A request names a transformer, attention, an encoder or decoder block, or asks to add or resize heads.
entries.source: Diagram by Daine Ball (Harold/GoSpark), shared 2026-08-06; standard architecture, independently derivable.
entries.verified_by: Shape algebra checked end to end against the diagram and against the reference formulation; no execution required for a shape invariant.

entries.lesson: RoPE encodes position by ROTATING each consecutive pair of dimensions rather than adding a position vector. For pair i at position m: theta_i = base^(-2i/d), angle = m * theta_i, and (x0, x1) -> (x0*cos - x1*sin, x0*sin + x1*cos). Applied to Q and K before the dot product, so d/2 independent 2D rotations per token.
entries.why_it_generalizes: Three consequences follow from the rotation being orthogonal, and each is a design constraint rather than a detail: position becomes RELATIVE (the QK dot product depends on m-n, not on m and n separately), vector MAGNITUDE is preserved (so it cannot destabilise attention the way an additive signal can), and it adds NO learned parameters.
implied_requirements: apply to Q and K only -- rotating V destroys the values being averaged
apply before the dot product, not after; rotating scores is not the same operation
d_head must be even, since the scheme consumes dimensions in pairs
base (commonly 10000) sets the frequency spread and therefore the usable context length
entries.reference: theta_i = base ** (-2*i/d);  angle = m * theta_i;  x0' = x0*cos(angle) - x1*sin(angle);  x1' = x0*sin(angle) + x1*cos(angle)
entries.used_when: A request mentions position encoding, context length, RoPE, sequence extrapolation, or asks why a model degrades past its trained length.
entries.source: Diagram by Daine Ball (Harold/GoSpark), shared 2026-08-06, showing the Go -> cgo -> rope kernel -> attention path.
entries.verified_by: Rotation matrix derived and checked: the form given is the standard 2x2 rotation, orthogonality confirmed (magnitude preserved), and the relative-position property follows from R(m)^T R(n) = R(n-m). Executed over worked pairs to confirm the sign convention matches.

entries.lesson: A request for a model component names roughly a third of what the component requires. 'Add attention' does not say causal or bidirectional, how many heads, whether positions are encoded, or what happens at the sequence boundary -- yet each choice changes the output and none of them cause an error.
entries.why_it_generalizes: This is the general shape of an under-specified build request, not a fact about transformers. The correct response is to enumerate the implied requirements and confirm or default them EXPLICITLY, because the failure mode is a component that runs, trains, and is quietly wrong -- which no compiler oracle catches.
implied_requirements: masking: causal or full, and what the padding positions do
position signal: none, learned, sinusoidal, or rotary
head count and whether d_model divides by it
normalisation placement: pre-norm or post-norm, which changes training stability
entries.used_when: Any generated-code request naming a model component, before generation rather than after a failure.
entries.source: Distilled from the two diagrams above plus the pattern the oracle work already documents.
entries.verified_by: Not a mathematical claim; recorded as a requirements heuristic. Its value is testable in use: does naming these before generation reduce silently-wrong output.
